Logging and Journaling

Learn to inspect classic /var/log files, query the systemd journal, and automate rotation with logrotate so logs stay useful and safe.

What you'll understand
How to find and interpret logs, query structured journal entries, and keep logs rotated and compressed.
Why it matters
Logs let you quickly root-cause outages, audit access, and spot faulty services before they cause outages.
In this lesson
We will move from reading /var/log files to using journalctl filters and finishing with a practical logrotate exercise you can run in a lab.
Concept map
Traditional logs
Plain text files under /var/log for services and the kernel.
systemd journal
Binary, structured logs that can be filtered by metadata.
Log rotation
Compressed archives and retention using logrotate policies.
Explore Key Topics
/var/log files — Look for syslog, auth, kern, and application logs to trace events and errors.
journalctl — Query by service, priority, PID, or time range for focused troubleshooting.
logrotate — Automate rotation, compression, and archive retention to protect disk space.

screens.title: System logs: the administrator's sensors
screens.narratorSegment: System logs are continuous records of events produced by the kernel, services, and applications. They capture timestamps, process identifiers, severity levels, and message text that document what the system did and when. For an administrator, logs are the primary evidence when a service fails, when a user authenticates, or when a hardware error occurs. A clear concrete example is a failed SSH login recorded in auth. log with a timestamp and source IP. That single line can show whether a brute-force attack is happening. A common misconception is that logs are only for debugging; in reality, they are also essential for security audits and capacity planning. Logs tell you not just that a failure occurred, but patterns over time that reveal creeping problems. Always consider retention and accessibility: if you delete logs too aggressively, you lose audit trails. The takeaway is that logs are both an operational tool and an audit record. Treat them as data you can query, retain, and protect. System logs: the administrator's sensors means treat logs as structured evidence for troubleshooting, auditing, and long-term analysis.. In practical terms, what logs capture and why they matter for operations and security. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › System logs
Definition

What system logs contain

Timestamps, facility or service name, severity, PID, and message text. These fields form the minimum evidence you need to diagnose events.

Concrete example
An auth.log entry showing a failed SSH attempt with timestamp and source IP is enough to start investigating unauthorized access.
Common mistake
Opening huge logs in a GUI editor. Use tail, less, or grep to avoid resource issues.
Key Takeaway

Logs are actionable data. Preserve them, query them, and use them as evidence during incidents.

Analogy
Think of logs as a black box recorder for a server. Each line is a timestamped event you can replay to understand cause and effect.
Sample auth log snippet
Oct 10 09:12:45 host sshd[1234]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 53722 ssh2
Oct 10 09:12:47 host sshd[1234]: Accepted password for alice from 203.0.113.5 port 43721 ssh2
Why this matters
Identify attacks fast and record evidence for audits.
Check
Can you find a failed and a successful login for the same service? That contrast helps pinpoint cause.

screens.title: Traditional syslog and /var/log files
screens.narratorSegment: Most systems keep plain text log files under /var/log. These are often written by a syslog daemon such as rsyslog or syslog-ng and grouped by purpose. For example, syslog or messages contain general system activity. auth. log or secure records authentication events like logins and sudo usage. kern. log and dmesg show kernel-level messages, useful for hardware or driver problems. boot. log captures startup messages, while application logs often live under service-specific subdirectories such as /var/log/apache2 or /var/log/nginx. To inspect these files efficiently, use tail -f to follow incoming entries and grep to filter keywords. less is useful when you need to page through history. A typical mistake is to assume all services write to a single file; many have their own logs with different formats. If you need to investigate an outage, check timestamps across syslog, auth, and application logs to correlate events. That cross-checking is how you build a timeline of what happened. Traditional syslog and /var/log files means check service-specific files plus syslog, auth, kern, and boot to build a timeline of events.. In practical terms, common log files and what they record. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Traditional syslog
Common files
  • /var/log/messages or /var/log/syslog — general system activity and informational messages.
  • /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure — authentication and sudo events.
  • /var/log/kern.log & /var/log/dmesg — kernel and boot-time messages.
  • Application directories like /var/log/nginx/ contain server-specific logs.
Terminal tips
ls -lh /var/log
tail -f /var/log/auth.log
grep "error" /var/log/messages
less /var/log/kern.log
Scenario

If a web request fails, check the web server access and error logs, then cross-reference system logs for related kernel or resource events. Correlate timestamps to trace the sequence.

Misconception
Logs are uniform across services. In practice formats and locations vary, so look for service-specific directories.
Key Takeaway

Use the right file for the right question. Start with service logs, then expand to system and kernel logs when needed.

screens.title: Using tail, grep, and less
screens.narratorSegment: When working with traditional text logs, a small set of commands provides most of your needs. tail -f shows incoming messages in real time, which is useful when you recreate an event to observe its log entry. grep filters a log for keywords such as error or failed, helping you find patterns quickly. less paginates large files and allows backward and forward navigation without loading the entire file into memory. Combine them: grep "failed" /var/log/auth. log | less shows matching lines in a pager. Use head to view the start of a file and tail -n to get the last N lines. A common mistake is to edit large logs in a text editor that loads the whole file; this can hang the system. content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › tail | grep | less
Code walkthrough
Run these commands to inspect and filter logs without opening them in an editor.
tail -f /var/log/auth.log
# follow live authentication events

grep "error" /var/log/messages | less
# filter by keyword and page through results

less /var/log/kern.log
# inspect large kernel logs with search and navigation

tail -n 50 /var/log/syslog
# show the last 50 lines
Scenario
Open tail -f and attempt an SSH login to generate entries you can watch in real time.
Mistake to avoid
Editing huge logs in GUI editors which may freeze your workstation or cause delays.
Practical tip

Open a second terminal to generate events while tail -f runs. Use grep as a quick sieve before piping to less for more context.

Key Takeaway

Use the right tool for the job: follow, filter, and page instead of editing huge log files.

screens.title: systemd-journald and structured logging
screens.narratorSegment: systemd's journald collects messages from the kernel, services' standard output and error, and early boot messages into a single structured, binary journal. Structured means each entry stores metadata such as PID, UID, service name, and timestamps as fields you can query. This differs from plain-text syslog which stores free-form lines that you must parse. The advantages are query precision and centralized history across boots. Another benefit is efficiency: binary storage can pack entries more compactly than many text files. journald also improves security by making tampering more difficult when proper filesystem permissions are used. A common contrast is that text logs are easy to read and archive with standard tools, while the journal requires journalctl to inspect. Both systems can coexist: journald can forward messages to syslog daemons. The practical skill is knowing when to prefer journalctl for fast metadata queries and when to check plain-text files for legacy or application-specific logs. systemd-journald and structured logging means the journal stores metadata-rich, binary entries that are queryable; classic logs are plain text and service-specific.. In practical terms, how journald differs from classic syslog. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › systemd-journald
Definition

What journald provides

  • Structured, binary storage of log entries with metadata fields.
  • Centralized collection from kernel, services, and early boot.
  • Queryable with journalctl by field, priority, service, or time.
Why prefer it
For precise filtering and retaining boot-to-boot history in one place.
Comparison
Journal
Binary, structured, queryable, centralized.
Syslog
Plain text files, simple to archive, service-specific locations.
Misconception
Journal replaces all logs. It complements them and can forward entries to syslog for compatibility.

screens.title: journalctl basics
screens.narratorSegment: journalctl is the primary tool to query systemd's journal. Running journalctl with no options prints all entries from oldest to newest. To watch new entries in real time, use journalctl -f, which behaves like tail -f but for the structured journal. You can filter by unit with -u followed by the service name, for example -u sshd to get only SSH daemon messages. Time-based filtering with --since and --until lets you narrow a period for incident analysis. Use -p with priority names such as err or crit to focus on higher-severity messages. You can filter by metadata fields too, for example _PID to find entries from a particular process. For disk management, journalctl --disk-usage shows journal consumption, and --vacuum-size or --vacuum-time reduce retained entries. A concrete command you will use: journalctl -u sshd -p err --since "02:00 today" --until "03:00 today" to find critical sshd messages in a time window. Practice combining selectors to find the exact entries you need. journalctl basics means use -u, -p, _pid, and --since/--until to locate exact log entries by metadata and time.. In practical terms, commands to view, follow, and filter the systemd journal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › journalctl basics
Quick commands
journalctl
journalctl -f
journalctl -u sshd
journalctl --since "2 hours ago"
journalctl -p err
journalctl _PID=1234
journalctl -n 20
These commands combine filters. For example, adding -u sshd with -p err returns error-level SSH messages only. Use -n to limit results when scanning recent history.
Disk control
Check usage with --disk-usage and reduce history with --vacuum-size or --vacuum-time to keep the journal within space limits.
Example
Find critical sshd messages between 02:00 and 03:00 using journalctl -u sshd -p crit --since "02:00 today" --until "03:00 today".
Key Takeaway

journalctl's structured filters let you target entries precisely. Combine selectors to reduce noise and find root causes faster.

screens.title: Journalctl filters vs. grep
screens.narratorSegment: Both journalctl and classic text tools have a place. Use journalctl when entries include metadata you want to filter by, such as service name, PID, UID, or priority. Journalctl queries those fields directly and returns precisely matching entries. For example, filtering by _PID returns only messages from a process without false positives. Use grep and tail when working with plain-text application logs in /var/log, or when you need to search for a free-form message across many files. A typical workflow might start with journalctl -u to find a service-level error and then switch to an application log directory to grep for correlated messages. A common misconception is that grep is always faster; in many cases journalctl with field filters is both faster and more accurate because it avoids irrelevant matches. Pick the tool that matches the data format and the question you need to answer. Journalctl filters vs. grep means use journalctl for metadata queries and grep/tail for raw text logs that lack structured fields..   • Query by unit, priority, PID, UID, and time fields.
  • Centralized journal across boots and services.
  • Avoids false matches on metadata fields.
Example
journalctl -u sshd -p err --since "yesterday"
Grep advantage
  • Simple text search across many plain files.
  • Works on legacy application logs and archives.
  • Combines with tail and less for live viewing and paging.
Example
grep -i "timeout" /var/log/nginx/*.log | less
Key Takeaway

Start with structured queries when possible, then use text tools for service-specific or archived logs.

screens.title: logrotate: purpose and architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Logrotate is a utility that automates rotating, compressing, and removing old log files according to policy. Its main configuration file is /etc/logrotate. conf, which sets defaults and includes additional rules from /etc/logrotate. d. Each application can have a file under /etc/logrotate. d that defines how to rotate its logs. Typical directives include rotate to set the number of archived files to keep, daily/weekly/monthly for frequency, size to trigger rotation by size, compress and delaycompress to manage compression, and postrotate/endscript to run commands after rotation. For example, many services require a signal or graceful restart so they reopen a new log file. Logrotate is usually invoked daily by cron, so it acts as a scheduled maintenance task. Misconfigurations can cause logs to stop rotating or be removed unexpectedly, so always test configurations with debug and force options before deploying to production. logrotate: purpose and architecture means logrotate applies written policies to compress and archive logs, preventing uncontrolled growth.. In practical terms, how logrotate manages growth and retention. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › logrotate overview
Where configs live
  • /etc/logrotate.conf — global defaults and includes.
  • /etc/logrotate.d/ — application-specific rotation rules.
Key directives let you control retention, frequency, compression, and post-rotation actions. Test with debug and force options to validate behavior safely.
Common directives
rotate N — Keep N old log files
daily / weekly / monthly — Rotate on a schedule
size SIZE — Rotate when the file grows past SIZE
compress / delaycompress — Compress archives and optionally delay compression
postrotate / endscript — Run commands after rotating

screens.title: Writing a logrotate rule
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a logrotate rule is straightforward. You place a file in /etc/logrotate. d that names the log and lists directives. In the example lab, a file targets /tmp/mylog. log, sets rotate 2 to keep two archives, size 1k to rotate when small, and compress to gzip old files. Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › logrotate example
Sample /etc/logrotate.d/mylog
/tmp/mylog.log {
    rotate 2
    size 1k
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 root root
}
Add content until the file exceeds 1k, then test using debug: sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/mylog. When ready, force a rotation with sudo logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/mylog and check /tmp for rotated compressed files.
Post-rotation action
If an application keeps a file descriptor open, include postrotate and a command to reopen logs, such as a graceful service reload.
Testing tips
  • Use -d to debug without changing files.
  • Use -f to force rotation when testing.
  • Confirm created file permissions with ls -l after rotation.
Key Takeaway

A tested rule prevents surprises in production. Always validate behavior and cleanup test configs.

screens.title: Running journal maintenance and vacuuming
screens.narratorSegment: Large journals can consume significant disk space if left unconstrained. Use journalctl --disk-usage to see how much space the journal consumes. To reduce usage, use vacuum commands: --vacuum-size retains journals until the total size is below the specified threshold, and --vacuum-time removes entries older than the given timespan. For example, journalctl --vacuum-size=1G keeps the journal under one gigabyte. Be cautious: vacuuming permanently removes old entries. Another option is to set SystemMaxUse or SystemKeepFree in journald. conf to control retention automatically. A misconception is that vacuuming is reversible; it is not. Always check disk-usage and plan retention according to your auditing needs before deleting history. For production systems, coordinate journal retention with organizational log retention policies and downstream log aggregation if required. Running journal maintenance and vacuuming means use --disk-usage and vacuum options to cap journal storage; consider journald.conf settings for ongoing limits.. In practical terms, controlling journal disk usage and retention. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Starter commands
ls -lh /var/log
# observe sizes and timestamps

screens.title: Common mistakes and mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes cause trouble when managing logs. First, opening very large logs in a GUI editor can hang your workstation; prefer tail, less, and grep. Second, misconfigured logrotate rules may not rotate files or may leave services writing to removed inodes; always include postrotate steps when services require reopening files and test with debug mode. Third, vacuuming the journal without confirming retention policy can destroy required audit history; coordinate with compliance before pruning. Fourth, assuming journald replaces all syslog files can hide application-specific plain text logs; check both the journal and /var/log locations. Mitigations are simple: test rotation configs, use force and debug flags to preview behavior, set journald. conf limits for ongoing retention, and maintain an external log aggregation pipeline for long-term storage when audits require it. These practices keep logs accessible, useful, and safe for investigations. Mistakes
  • Editing huge logs in GUI editors rather than using tail/less.
  • Not using postrotate causing services to keep writing to old inodes.
  • Pruning journal history without confirming audit requirements.
  • Assuming all logs are available only in the journal when some remain in /var/log.
Mitigations
  • Use tail, grep, and less for large files and live observation.
  • Test logrotate configurations with -d and -f before applying to production.
  • Configure journald.conf or use vacuum commands carefully and after approval.
  • Keep both journal and plain-text logs in scope when searching for entries.

Anticipate service behavior during rotation and coordinate retention with auditing needs to prevent data loss.

fullNarratorScript:
Logs are the primary source of truth about what happened on a Linux system. In this chapter you will learn to read traditional text logs in /var/log, leverage systemd's structured journal with journalctl, and configure automatic log rotation with logrotate to prevent disk exhaustion. You will see concrete commands for live troubleshooting, learn how journalctl filters make queries precise, and practice a small lab that creates a dummy log and forces a rotation. Understanding logs means faster incident diagnosis, reliable security auditing, and predictable disk use. We'll emphasize common mistakes to avoid, like opening massive files in a text editor or misconfiguring rotation directives that leave services writing to deleted files. By the end, you will be able to find critical messages, limit journal disk usage, and craft a logrotate policy that matches operational needs. Consider how quickly you could resolve an outage if you can filter by service, priority, or time range. Keep that goal in mind as we explore each topic in detail.

These objectives focus your practice and show what competency looks like. First, you will learn why system logs are critical for troubleshooting, security auditing, and performance monitoring. You will practice interpreting messages that reveal the root cause of failures. Second, you will locate and read common traditional log files in /var/log; you will identify the purpose of messages in files such as syslog, auth. log, kern. log, and dmesg. Third, you will use journalctl to query and filter systemd's journal with time ranges, service selectors, priority levels, and process IDs. You will see how structured fields make queries precise. Fourth, you will configure logrotate to rotate, compress, and retain logs according to policy. You will write a sample configuration and force a rotation to observe results. Each objective pairs a practical command set with a reason why the skill prevents outages or data loss. Practice these until you can find and preserve the exact log entries you need for incident reports and audits.

In the lab you will demonstrate each objective with commands and a configuration file. For logs, you will show you can find authentication attempts in auth. log and interpret timestamps and IP addresses. For traditional logs, you will run tail -f and grep to filter messages and explain why less or tail are preferable to opening large files in an editor. For the systemd journal, you will compose journalctl filters that return only the service entries you need, and you will interpret structured fields like _PID or _UID. For logrotate, you will author a config in /etc/logrotate. d, test the configuration in debug mode, and perform a forced rotation to confirm the expected rotated and compressed files exist. Each milestone ties a command to an outcome: recover the cause of a failed service, produce audit evidence of a login, or prevent disk exhaustion by validating rotation policies. These concrete demonstrations show you are ready to operate logs in production.

System logs are continuous records of events produced by the kernel, services, and applications. They capture timestamps, process identifiers, severity levels, and message text that document what the system did and when. For an administrator, logs are the primary evidence when a service fails, when a user authenticates, or when a hardware error occurs. A clear concrete example is a failed SSH login recorded in auth. log with a timestamp and source IP. That single line can show whether a brute-force attack is happening. A common misconception is that logs are only for debugging; in reality, they are also essential for security audits and capacity planning. Logs tell you not just that a failure occurred, but patterns over time that reveal creeping problems. Always consider retention and accessibility: if you delete logs too aggressively, you lose audit trails. The takeaway is that logs are both an operational tool and an audit record. Treat them as data you can query, retain, and protect. System logs: the administrator's sensors means treat logs as structured evidence for troubleshooting, auditing, and long-term analysis.. In practical terms, what logs capture and why they matter for operations and security. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Most systems keep plain text log files under /var/log. These are often written by a syslog daemon such as rsyslog or syslog-ng and grouped by purpose. For example, syslog or messages contain general system activity. auth. log or secure records authentication events like logins and sudo usage. kern. log and dmesg show kernel-level messages, useful for hardware or driver problems. boot. log captures startup messages, while application logs often live under service-specific subdirectories such as /var/log/apache2 or /var/log/nginx. To inspect these files efficiently, use tail -f to follow incoming entries and grep to filter keywords. less is useful when you need to page through history. A typical mistake is to assume all services write to a single file; many have their own logs with different formats. If you need to investigate an outage, check timestamps across syslog, auth, and application logs to correlate events. That cross-checking is how you build a timeline of what happened. Traditional syslog and /var/log files means check service-specific files plus syslog, auth, kern, and boot to build a timeline of events.. In practical terms, common log files and what they record. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When working with traditional text logs, a small set of commands provides most of your needs. tail -f shows incoming messages in real time, which is useful when you recreate an event to observe its log entry. grep filters a log for keywords such as error or failed, helping you find patterns quickly. less paginates large files and allows backward and forward navigation without loading the entire file into memory. Combine them: grep "failed" /var/log/auth. log | less shows matching lines in a pager. Use head to view the start of a file and tail -n to get the last N lines. A common mistake is to edit large logs in a text editor that loads the whole file; this can hang the system. For live troubleshooting, open a second terminal to run tail -f while you trigger the event in the first. Practice these commands until they feel natural; they form the foundation for log triage. Using tail, grep, and less means tail, grep, and less let you follow, filter, and page through logs without heavy editors.. In practical terms, efficient commands to inspect and filter text logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

systemd's journald collects messages from the kernel, services' standard output and error, and early boot messages into a single structured, binary journal. Structured means each entry stores metadata such as PID, UID, service name, and timestamps as fields you can query. This differs from plain-text syslog which stores free-form lines that you must parse. The advantages are query precision and centralized history across boots. journalctl is the primary tool to query systemd's journal. Running journalctl with no options prints all entries from oldest to newest. To watch new entries in real time, use journalctl -f, which behaves like tail -f but for the structured journal. You can filter by unit with -u followed by the service name, for example -u sshd to get only SSH daemon messages. Time-based filtering with --since and --until lets you narrow a period for incident analysis. Use -p with priority names such as err or crit to focus on higher-severity messages. You can filter by metadata fields too, for example _PID to find entries from a particular process. For disk management, journalctl --disk-usage shows journal consumption, and --vacuum-size or --vacuum-time reduce retained entries. A concrete command you will use: journalctl -u sshd -p err --since "02:00 today" --until "03:00 today" to find critical sshd messages in a time window. Both journalctl and classic text tools have a place. Use journalctl when entries include metadata you want to filter by, such as service name, PID, UID, or priority. Journalctl queries those fields directly and returns precisely matching entries. For example, filtering by _PID returns only messages from a process without false positives. Use grep and tail when working with plain-text application logs in /var/log, or when you need to search for a free-form message across many files. A typical workflow might start with journalctl -u to find a service-level error and then switch to an application log directory to grep for correlated messages. Logrotate is a utility that automates rotating, compressing, and removing old log files according to policy. Its main configuration file is /etc/logrotate. conf, which sets defaults and includes additional rules from /etc/logrotate. d. Each application can have a file under /etc/logrotate. d that defines how to rotate its logs. Typical directives include rotate to set the number of archived files to keep, daily/weekly/monthly for frequency, size to trigger rotation by size, compress and delaycompress to manage compression, and postrotate/endscript to run commands after rotation. For example, many services require a signal or graceful restart so they reopen a new log file. Logrotate is usually invoked daily by cron, so it acts as a scheduled maintenance task. Large journals can consume significant disk space if left unconstrained. Use journalctl --disk-usage to see how much space the journal consumes. To reduce usage, use vacuum commands: --vacuum-size retains journals until the total size is below the specified threshold, and --vacuum-time removes entries older than the given timespan. For example, journalctl --vacuum-size=1G keeps the journal under one gigabyte. Be cautious: vacuuming permanently removes old entries. Another option is to set SystemMaxUse or SystemKeepFree in journald. conf to control retention automatically. A misconception is that vacuuming is reversible; it is not. Always check disk-usage and plan retention according to your auditing needs before deleting history. For production systems, coordinate journal retention with organizational log retention policies and downstream log aggregation if required. Several recurring mistakes cause trouble when managing logs. First, opening very large logs in a GUI editor can hang your workstation; prefer tail, less, and grep. Second, misconfigured logrotate rules may not rotate files or may leave services writing to removed inodes; always include postrotate steps when services require reopening files and test with debug mode. Third, vacuuming the journal without confirming retention policy can destroy required audit history; coordinate with compliance before pruning. Fourth, assuming journald replaces all syslog files can hide application-specific plain text logs; check both the journal and /var/log locations. Mitigations are simple: test rotation configs, use force and debug flags to preview behavior, set journald. conf limits for ongoing retention, and maintain an external log aggregation pipeline for long-term storage when audits require it. These practices keep logs accessible, useful, and safe for investigations. Here are three central ideas to keep in your toolkit. First, system logs are indispensable for troubleshooting and auditing; they record events with timestamps and metadata that let you reconstruct incidents. Second, systemd's journal adds structured fields that make querying precise, but plain-text files under /var/log remain important for many applications. Third, automated rotation with logrotate prevents uncontrolled log growth; write and test rotation policies and use postrotate when services must reopen files. Memorize these concepts and use them together: inspect logs to form hypotheses, use journalctl for focused queries, and ensure rotation policies preserve important history while keeping disk use predictable.
